This walkthrough picks up where [Get started](RiboPilot.html) leaves off.

By clicking **Assign Taxonomy**, RiboPilot matches each Taxon in your mapping file to
the NCBI taxonomy database. The first time this runs, it downloads about 80 MB
and builds an index of about 0.5 GB inside the project, which takes a few
minutes.

The Confidence column says how well your taxon names matched the NCBI taxonomy database:

| Confidence | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| exact | Your taxon name matched exactly one NCBI taxon. | Nothing. |
| fuzzy_species | No exact match, so a species of the same genus with a very similar name was picked. | Check the spelling. |
| fuzzy_genus | Only the genus matched. | Check the name, and pick the species if NCBI has it. |
| ambiguous | The name matches more than one organism; for example, the genus *Morus* is both a mulberry and a gannet. No taxon is set. | Pick the right one. The Other Matches column lists each candidate with its kingdom. |
| unresolved | No match. | Pick a taxon by hand. |
| manual | You picked the taxon by hand. | Nothing. |

To pick a taxon by hand, click the sample's ID (or tick its row and press **Edit
Taxonomy**), search for the name, and press **Assign**.

It's important to carefully review the taxonomy for each of your samples.
A sample with incorrect taxonomic assignment here will be checked against the 
wrong taxonomic groups during assembly and annotation.

When finished, tick all rows and press **Lock**. Only samples whose taxonomy is locked go
on to the Assemble step. If you lock a sample that has no taxon, RiboPilot asks you first.

In the test project, all 12 test samples match exactly:

![Taxonomy step with all 12 test samples matched and locked](figures/get-started/taxonomy-locked.png)
